notes:
I worked from a limited set of pages. I read the full Enduring Word (Guzik) commentary, Wesley's *Notes*, Augustine's Tractate 49 and parts of Preceptaustin, Bible.org (Utley and an exegetical commentary that includes NET notes), Biblehub (Ellicott, Gill, Poole, Barnes, Meyer, Pulpit, Hastings), Barclay and Matthew Henry. I found nothing on catholic.com, oca.org or bibleodyssey.org, and no prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace material, so those are left out. Verse 28 is left out because I found nothing on it.

---

**v. 1**
- Guzik calls this perhaps Jesus' most remarkable miracle, the seventh sign in John. He quotes Barclay that there is no parallel for raising someone four days dead. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/
- Why the other Gospels leave it out: Guzik gives Grotius's guess (via Clarke) that they wrote while Lazarus was alive and didn't want to endanger him. He also gives Morris's guess that Peter wasn't there. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/ Wesley gives the same reason as Grotius. Here is the plain reason why the other evangelists, who wrote while Lazarus was living, did not relate his story. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-gospel-according-to-st-john/
- The name: "Lazarus" is the Hebrew name "Eleazer," which means "God helps" or "God is helper." Luke 10:38-42 is the only mention of them in the Synoptic Gospels. https://bible.org/book/export/html/19304
- Wesley thinks Lazarus was probably younger than his sisters. He adds that, according to church history, Lazarus was now thirty years old, and that he lived thirty years after Christ's ascension. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/11.htm
- **Other view (older scholarship):** Some have linked Lazarus with the poor man in Jesus' parable (Luke 16). Biblehub's commentaries record that Bishop Wordsworth and Archdeacon Watkins are disposed to identify the Lazarus of the parable and the Lazarus of Bethany. They also mention the theory that the story is a parable turned into a miracle. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/11-1.htm Barclay notes the same suggestion. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/john-11.html

**v. 2**
- Preceptaustin says John is making sure we know which Mary he means: the Mary of Bethany, since the New Testament has six Marys. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-11-commentary
- Wesley: She was more known than her elder sister Martha, and as such is named before her. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/11.htm
- **Catholic / Western patristic reading:** Augustine tentatively equates this Mary with the sinful woman of Luke 7 ("if, indeed, it was she"). He says she had a better resurrection than her brother; she was delivered from the mighty burden of a sinful character. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701049.htm

**v. 3**
- Guzik points out that the sisters didn't actually ask Jesus to come. They felt it was enough to tell Him the problem. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/ Augustine draws the same lesson: It is enough that You know; for You are not one that loves and forsakes. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701049.htm
- Spurgeon (Baptist): those Jesus loves do get ill, and the illness may even be sent by God as a token and testimony of his affection for them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-11-commentary

**v. 4**
- Guzik: Lazarus was already dead when Jesus said this, but Jesus knew the outcome would be God's glory. The events would also push the leaders toward killing Him, so the Son would be glorified through His death and resurrection. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/
- Wesley: the outcome will not be death, in the usual sense of the word, a final separation of his soul and body; but a manifestation of the glorious power of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/11.htm
- Bible.org's exegetical notes: the glory comes in the sense that it will lead to his death, which is a stage in his glorification. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-11
- **Scholarship (text):** Utley notes that the words "of God" in "Son of God" are not in the ancient Greek papyri manuscripts P^45 or P^66. https://bible.org/book/export/html/19304
- Augustine: this glorifying added nothing to Christ's dignity but benefited us. The death was unto the working of a miracle whereby men might be led to faith in Christ, and so escape the real death. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701049.htm
- Spurgeon: sickness has a limit. Lazarus might pass through death, but death was not to be the ultimatum of his sickness. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-11-commentary

**v. 5**
- Guzik: John adds this so we know the testing of their faith did not mean Jesus didn't love them. He quotes Morris that naming all three stresses that Jesus loved each one individually. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/
- Deffinbaugh: THE PURPOSE OF GOD IS NEVER SEPARATED FROM HIS LOVE FOR HIS OWN. https://bible.org/seriespage/13-resurrection-and-life-john-111-53
- Augustine: The one sick, the others sad, all of them beloved. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701049.htm

**v. 6**
- Guzik: the delay made the sisters' grief last longer. He notes a pattern in John: three times someone close to Jesus asks Him for something, and each time He first refuses, then acts on God's timetable. Delays are not denials. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/
- MacArthur: the delay strengthened the sisters' faith, made it clear Lazarus was truly dead, and kept Jesus on God's timetable. Steven Cole says Jesus' love was the very reason He stayed. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-11-commentary
- Matthew Henry: because He loved them, He planned something extraordinary and therefore he delayed coming to them, that Lazarus might be dead and buried before he came. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_011.cfm
- Augustine: He delayed to heal, that He might be able to raise to life. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701049.htm
- Bible.org's exegetical notes report that some have suggested Jesus deliberately waited for Lazarus to die. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-11

**v. 7**
- Guzik: Jesus could have raised Lazarus from a distance, but chose to go to dangerous Judea despite the disciples' warnings. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/
- Wesley: He left the country east of Jordan, whither he had retired some time before, when the Jews sought to stone him. https://ccel.org/ccel/wesley/notes.i.v.xii.html

**v. 8**
- Guzik: the disciples were shocked that Jesus would go back to a region where He was a wanted man. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/
- Augustine recalls that the Lord had escaped those trying to stone Him and gone beyond the Jordan. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701049.htm

**vv. 9–10**
- Guzik: the "twelve hours" stand for the time the Father had given for Jesus' earthly work. During those hours no harm could come to Him. He quotes Alford and Barclay. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/
- Wesley explains that the Jews divided daylight into twelve parts, so hours were shorter in winter. He reads Jesus as saying there is a determined time, which God has allotted me. On v. 10, walking at night means having no light from God, if his providence does no longer protect him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/11.htm
- A.T. Robertson: It is not blind fatalism that Jesus proclaims, but the opposite of cowardice. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-11-commentary

**v. 11**
- Guzik: "sleep" was a familiar picture of death, and especially fitting because Jesus would soon wake him. He compares Jairus' daughter and Stephen. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/
- Wesley: Jesus said this just as Lazarus died. "Sleep" is the death of good men in the language of heaven. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/11.htm
- Matthew Henry: Death itself does not break the bond of friendship between Christ and a believer. Calling death sleep makes it less frightening. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_011.cfm
- Lampe (cited by Preceptaustin): "our friend" goes further than "the one You love," because it shows Lazarus loved Jesus back. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-11-commentary
- Augustine: To his sisters he was dead, to the Lord he was asleep. He uses the verse to teach that at death the good immediately have joy and the evil torment, and that both become fuller at the resurrection. In other words, "sleep" does not mean the soul is unconscious. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701049.htm

**v. 12**
- Augustine: For the sleep of the sick is usually a sign of returning health. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701049.htm
- Spurgeon makes the same point, and adds that since even the apostles missed a figure of speech, preachers must speak plainly. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-11-commentary

**v. 13**
- Wesley: the disciples did not yet understand heaven's language. The slowness of our understanding makes the Scripture often descend to our barbarous manner of speaking. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/11.htm

**v. 14**
- Bible.org's exegetical notes: Jesus' plain statement is best seen as another case of his supernatural knowledge, since the messengers only brought word that Lazarus was sick. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-11

**v. 15**
- Bible.org's exegetical notes: His rejoicing is shocking, but He rejoices for the disciples' sake, because the miracle will lead them to believe. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-11
- Guzik: Jesus could be glad because He was sure of the outcome. He quotes Morgan that God sometimes lets us go through deeper darkness so we can see His power more fully. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/
- Augustine: the disciples already believed. The miracle increased a faith that already existed rather than starting it. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701049.htm
- Bengel: we read of no one having died while the Prince of life was present. On "let us go to him," Preceptaustin's commentator says death could not break Jesus' relationship with His friend. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-11-commentary

**v. 16**
- Guzik reports a church tradition that Thomas was called "the Twin" because he looked like Jesus. Barclay explains that "Thomas" is the Hebrew and "Didymus" the Greek word for twin. Tasker calls Thomas's words "a cry of loyal despair." Dods calls him the pessimist of the group, whose loyalty wouldn't let Jesus go alone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/
- Wesley says Thomas meant dying with Jesus, whom he expected the Jews to kill, and that It seems to be the language of despair. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/11.htm

**v. 17**
- Utley: The rabbis said that the human spirit stayed close to the physical body for three days. Jesus waited past this so Lazarus was clearly beyond hope. https://bible.org/book/export/html/19304
- Guzik quotes Ben Kaphra's tradition (via Dods and Lightfoot) and Clarke's timeline: Lazarus was probably buried on the day he died, or the day after. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/

**v. 18**
- Utley: this is one of John's editorial comments. The distance is literally "fifteen furlongs." https://bible.org/book/export/html/19304

**v. 19**
- Guzik: the crowd was still there four days on, because joining the mourners of a close relative was an important duty. He cites Tenney on Jewish mourning customs. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/
- Utley: this is an uncharacteristic neutral use of the term "the Jews," which usually in John refers to Jesus' enemies. https://bible.org/book/export/html/19304
- Wesley takes the visits of condolence as a sign that Martha was a person of some figure. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-gospel-according-to-st-john/

**v. 20**
- Guzik quotes Clarke: sitting was the ancient posture of mourners, as if grief had made them unable to move. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/
- Wesley's view is simpler: Mary was Probably not hearing what was said. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/11.htm

**v. 21**
- Guzik: Martha honestly states her disappointment. She believed Jesus could heal, but may not have imagined He could raise Lazarus now. He quotes Morgan that people treated death as unconquerable. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/
- Barclay notes that Mary later greets Jesus with exactly the same words (v. 32). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/john-11.html

**v. 22** *(interpreters differ on what Martha expected)*
- Wesley: So that she already believed he could raise him from the dead. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/11.htm
- Guzik disagrees. He thinks Martha was *not* confident of a raising, but was saying she would trust Jesus despite her disappointment. He applies it to "even now" prayers for situations that look hopeless. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/
- Maclaren (on Biblehub) sees her faith at a "lofty height" here, but says Jesus offers her an even higher view of who He is. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/11-25.htm

**v. 23**
- Guzik: when we comfort mourners with "you'll see him again," we don't mean right now, but Jesus did mean right now. He quotes Alford that the final resurrection happens by Christ's power, so He can raise now as well. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/

**v. 24**
- Guzik quotes Bruce that, thanks to the Pharisees, belief in the resurrection was by then common among Jews despite the Sadducees. He quotes Spurgeon that this distant hope gave Martha little comfort. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/
- Hastings: Martha treated the resurrection as a mere matter of destiny like birth and death, a distant mysterious event. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hastings/john/11-25.htm

**v. 25**
- Ellicott (Anglican): the emphasis means "I, and none beside Me" am the resurrection, which is a. present life, and not simply a life in the remoteness of the last day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/11-25.htm
- Guzik: Jesus doesn't claim to *have* resurrection or know its secrets. He *is* it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/
- Poole reads it as the effect standing for the cause: Jesus is the principal cause of the resurrection. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/11-25.htm
- Barnes: Faith does not save from temporal death; but although the believer, as others, will die a temporal death, yet he will hereafter have life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/11-25.htm
- Wesley: resurrection - Of the dead. And the life - Of the living. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/john/11.htm
- Gill (Baptist) also applies the verse to a spiritual resurrection, from a death of sin, to a life of grace, with Christ as its author through His Spirit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/11-25.htm
- Augustine reasons that the One by whom Lazarus will rise at the last day can raise him now. He also reads Lazarus as a picture of the habitual sinner, "buried" in sin. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701049.htm
- Biblehub's study note says the "I am" connect Jesus to the divine name revealed to Moses in Exodus 3:14. https://biblehub.com/study/john/11-25.htm

**v. 26**
- Guzik quotes Morris: Jesus doesn't mean believers won't die physically, but that they will not die in the sense in which death has eternal significance. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/
- Utley points to the present tenses ("believes," "lives"), which show belief must continue, and to the strong double negative, which he takes as referring to spiritual death. https://bible.org/book/export/html/19304
- **Scholarship:** Utley reads this as "realized eschatology": eternal life begins now for believers, and Lazarus illustrates Jesus' words. https://bible.org/book/export/html/19304 The Pulpit Commentary notes the Greek could instead be read as "not forever," which would point to the future resurrection. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/11-25.htm

**v. 27**
- Biblehub's word note: "Christ" is the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew "Messiah," meaning "Anointed One." https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/john/11.htm

---

**Where traditions differ:** In the pages I read, Baptist (Spurgeon, Gill, MacArthur), Methodist (Wesley), Presbyterian (Matthew Henry), Anglican (Ellicott) and Calvary Chapel (Guzik) writers mostly agree on the plain meaning. The real differences I found:
- **v. 22:** Wesley thinks Martha expected a raising; Guzik thinks she didn't.
- **v. 25:** Gill reads it as also describing regeneration from the death of sin; Wesley and Barnes keep to physical and eternal life.
- **v. 2:** Augustine tentatively identifies Mary of Bethany with the sinful woman of Luke 7; none of the Protestant pages I read do.
